# DATA-3 extensions — generated by `extend.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. Expedites — what to DO about a shortage

The first build identified shortage drivers and stopped there. An expedite recommendation is what a materials manager is actually asking for, and the number that decides it is **not the premium** — it is the premium against the margin of the units it unblocks. That comparison is hard in practice for a structural reason: the premium arrives on an invoice and the margin is not visible from the materials system at all.

| part | supplier | mode | lead mean | days saved | premium | recovers runway? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PRT-0111 | SUP-004 | air freight | 59 d | 33 d | $900 | no |
| PRT-0111 | SUP-004 | partial shipment | 59 d | 18 d | $240 | no |
| PRT-0111 | SUP-004 | supplier overtime | 59 d | 9 d | $75 | no |
| PRT-0042 | SUP-040 | air freight | 46 d | 25 d | $7,693 | **yes** |
| PRT-0042 | SUP-040 | partial shipment | 46 d | 14 d | $2,051 | **yes** |
| PRT-0042 | SUP-040 | supplier overtime | 46 d | 7 d | $641 | **yes** |
| PRT-0223 | SUP-031 | air freight | 69 d | 38 d | $574 | no |
| PRT-0223 | SUP-031 | partial shipment | 69 d | 21 d | $153 | no |
| PRT-0223 | SUP-031 | supplier overtime | 69 d | 10 d | $48 | no |
| PRT-0137 | SUP-048 | air freight | 60 d | 33 d | $2,350 | no |
| PRT-0137 | SUP-048 | partial shipment | 60 d | 18 d | $627 | no |
| PRT-0137 | SUP-048 | supplier overtime | 60 d | 9 d | $196 | no |

**12 of 24 options actually recover the runway** — i.e. the days saved exceed the days already lost past the order-by date. The rest are money spent on a part that will still be late, which is the expedite decision people get wrong most often: air freight on a part that needed ordering six weeks ago buys a faster arrival of something that is still after the line stops.

## 2. Multi-tier risk — the concentration nobody sees

**Dual-sourcing a part is worthless if both sources buy from the same sub-tier.** This is the failure that took out automotive semiconductors and aerospace castings repeatedly: the risk register said "dual sourced" and the dependency graph said otherwise, because nobody had the second tier.

| tier-2 source | tier-1 suppliers behind it | parts exposed | products affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| T2-01 | 13 | 63 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-02 | 9 | 51 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-03 | 7 | 42 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-05 | 7 | 36 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-12 | 4 | 15 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-09 | 2 | 15 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-04 | 3 | 12 | 4 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-C, PRD-D) |
| T2-10 | 2 | 8 | 3 (PRD-A, PRD-B, PRD-D) |

**T2-01 sits behind 13 tier-1 suppliers, 63 parts, and 4 of the product line.** A single-tier risk score cannot see that number, because at tier 1 those parts are spread across many independent-looking vendors.

Tier-1 suppliers a buyer would treat as alternatives, that in fact converge:

| tier-2 | tier-1 suppliers sharing it | parts exposed |
|---|---|---|
| T2-01 | 13 (SUP-002, SUP-006, SUP-007, SUP-008, SUP-014, SUP-016) | 63 |
| T2-02 | 9 (SUP-010, SUP-015, SUP-017, SUP-018, SUP-033, SUP-035) | 51 |
| T2-05 | 7 (SUP-003, SUP-005, SUP-013, SUP-029, SUP-030, SUP-032) | 36 |
| T2-03 | 7 (SUP-004, SUP-011, SUP-022, SUP-024, SUP-027, SUP-039) | 42 |
| T2-12 | 4 (SUP-009, SUP-012, SUP-026, SUP-047) | 15 |
| T2-04 | 3 (SUP-023, SUP-025, SUP-036) | 12 |

**Honest scope:** the tier-2 mapping is *generated*, not discovered. In reality it is the hardest data in this whole project to obtain — suppliers treat their own sources as confidential, and the mapping is assembled from questionnaires, customs records and industry knowledge, then goes stale. The analysis here shows what the data buys once you have it; getting it is the actual work and it is not a modelling problem.

## 3. Calibration — the real version

RESULTS.md §2 checked what fraction of simulations fell below their own P50, and said outright that this verifies arithmetic rather than the model. This is the honest test: draw **60 independent futures** from the generative process, treat each as what actually happened, and ask how often the forecast fan (built from 150 simulations) contained it.

| product | % inside P10–P90 | % below P10 | % above P90 | target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PRD-A | **98.8%** | 0.0% | 1.2% | 80% |
| PRD-B | **100.0%** | 0.0% | 0.0% | 80% |
| PRD-C | **99.1%** | 0.0% | 0.9% | 80% |
| PRD-D | **97.3%** | 0.0% | 2.7% | 80% |

**Mean coverage: 98.8% against a target of 80%.**

The band is **too wide**. An interval that contains the outcome far more often than advertised is not conservative-and-therefore-safe: it is a forecast nobody will plan against, because the P10 stops being a meaningful floor. The likely cause is that the fan and the futures are drawn from the same lead-time distributions, so the only variation the fan sees is the variation it was built from — a real fan also has to carry parameter uncertainty, which would widen the *true* outcome spread rather than the predicted one.

This is still a calibration against *my own generator*, and that limit is irreducible without real receipt history: the futures and the fan share a data-generating process, so what is verified is internal consistency of the propagation, not that supplier lead times behave this way.

## 4. The weekly materials pack

Generated to `out/materials_review_pack.md` — the artifact the Monday meeting runs on, produced by code rather than assembled by hand at 7 a.m. Four sections: can we build the plan, top shortage drivers with order-by dates, recommended expedites with costs, and sub-tier concentration.

The design rule for this document is that **every row implies an action or it does not belong**. A materials pack that reports status without naming the decision is the thing that makes the meeting an hour long and the decisions late.
